title.en: Check the conserved quantity across the domain

summary: Derive downstream quantities from the conservation law and verify that what enters the domain leaves or accumulates.
objective: Give a flow or transport scene a check that reveals leaks in the model.
applies_when: Fluid, heat or material moves through a conduit, network or region.
Cross-section, velocity or flow rate is displayed.
The scene claims that flow speeds up or slows down for a physical reason.
intent_signals: why does it speed up in the nozzle
example_prompts: Show why flow accelerates through the narrow section.
Check that the flow into the network equals the flow out.
negative_signals: Compressible or high-speed flows, where the simple relation does not hold.
Decorative particle streams that model no transport.
not_for: Compressible or high-speed flows, where the simple relation does not hold.
Decorative particle streams that model no transport.

principles: Conservation is the strongest available check on a transport model. For steady incompressible flow with no sources or sinks, the volume flow rate is the cross-sectional area times the cross-section-averaged normal speed, and that product is the same at every section, so a narrower section carries a faster average speed. Heat and material transport with sources, storage or reactions need their own balance with those terms, not this area-speed equality.
A visual that shows particles speeding up without preserving the product is showing an effect without its cause, and it will disagree with any number the scene displays.
Balance also localises errors: checking inflow against outflow plus accumulation identifies where the model is leaking rather than merely reporting that it does.
The assumptions matter: incompressibility and the absence of sources or sinks are the conditions under which the simple relation applies.
implementation: Compute the downstream speed from the conservation relation and the geometry rather than authoring it, so the visual follows the physics.
Display the conserved quantity and its units, and show it staying constant across the sections.
For a network, report inflow, outflow and accumulation per node and highlight any imbalance.
State the assumptions, including incompressibility and the absence of sources and sinks, next to the display.

Say what your particles are. Equal-volume tracers emitted at a fixed rate into a steady flow correctly encode flux, and their spacing stretches where the flow accelerates; illustrative particles seeded for visual density encode nothing quantitative and should be labelled that way. Streamline density is a third convention with its own seeding rule.
observable_checks: Measure the product of area and cross-section-averaged normal speed at several sections of a steady incompressible conduit flow with no leaks and confirm it is constant within tolerance.
Change the constriction and confirm the downstream speed changes by the expected factor.
Sum inflows and outflows over a closed region and confirm the balance holds.

Confirm the particle scheme matches its stated meaning: fixed-rate equal-volume tracers should keep a constant count crossing each section per unit time while their spacing changes with speed, and a decorative emitter should not be presented as a flux measurement.

creative_affordances: The visual language for flow, whether particles, ribbons, arrows or colour, is a free choice above the conservation check.
Deliberately stylised flow is fine when no rate is claimed.
known_limits: Authored validation guidance citing the incompressible continuity relation; compressible, unsteady and turbulent flows are outside it.
No fluid simulation has been run for this record.

claims.statement: For an incompressible fluid with no sources or sinks the volume flow rate equals cross-sectional area times the average speed and is the same at every section of a conduit, so the product of area and average speed at one section equals that product at another.
claims.scope: Steady incompressible flow in a conduit with the speed taken as the cross-section average of the normal component. Compressible, unsteady or source-bearing transport requires additional terms.

source_refs.locator: 14.5, flow rate and its relation to velocity, equation of continuity
